content: Tallow is a processed form of fat derived from beef or mutton, specifically rendered from suet. Unlike suet, tallow has the advantage of being storable for long periods without refrigeration, as long as it is kept in an airtight container to prevent oxidation. In contrast, rendered fat from pigs is referred to as lard. Tallow has a variety of applications. It is commonly used in animal feed, soap production, cooking, and as bird food. Additionally, it serves as a raw material in the production of biodiesel and other oleochemicals. Historically, tallow was utilized in the manufacture of tallow candles, which were a more economical alternative to wax candles. In industrial contexts, tallow is not strictly limited to beef or mutton fat; it is defined by specific technical criteria, such as its melting point, also known as its titre. Commercially available tallow often includes fat from other animals, such as pigs. In the 1990s, concerns arose regarding the high cholesterol content of tallow, as well as ethical objections from Hindus (many of whom avoid beef-derived products) and vegetarians. During this time, McDonald’s french fries were cooked in a mixture of 93% beef tallow and 7% cottonseed oil. In the steel rolling industry, tallow is used as a lubricant to facilitate the compression of sheet steel through rollers. However, there is a growing trend toward replacing tallow-based lubricants with synthetic oils to improve surface cleanliness during rolling processes. Tallow can also function as a flux in soldering applications. The fatty acid composition of tallow is as follows: Saturated fatty acids: Palmitic acid: 26% Stearic acid: 14% Myristic acid: 3% Monounsaturated fatty acids: Oleic acid: 47% Palmitoleic acid: 3% Polyunsaturated fatty acids: Linoleic acid: 3% Linolenic acid: 1%
